---
title: "How This Course Works"
subtitle: "MCEN 3021 Fluid Mechanics"
---

This course runs on **peer instruction**. The short version: you meet the
ideas *before* class, we spend class time arguing about them, and you apply
them *after* class with professional-style analysis tools. Here is the loop,
and your part in it:

**Before class — read one module (20-30 min).** Each module on this site is
one class meeting: a short reading built around **one big idea**, a live
demo you can play with (the Python runs in your browser — nothing to
install), and a few check questions. Do the LMS reading quiz before the
deadline; it is graded on effort, not correctness. *It is fine — expected,
even — to arrive confused about the hard part. It is not fine to arrive
blank.*

**In class — vote, argue, vote again.** Class is built around concept
questions. You will commit to an answer, then convince your neighbor (or be
convinced), then vote again. The research on this is unambiguous: the
explaining is where the learning happens. Bring your phone for voting.

**After class — verify, then apply.** Homework pairs one handwritten
calculation with a bigger analysis using the course toolbox
(`fluidtools`, a Python package you will run in Colab). The handwritten part
proves the tool — and you — are right; the tool part does what professionals
do: real systems, real design questions.

::: {.callout-note}
## First load on each page takes ~15-30 seconds
The scientific Python stack downloads to your browser once per page and is
cached afterward. Live cells have a *Run Code* button; edit anything and hit
*Start Over* if you break it. You cannot hurt anything.
:::

## Where things live

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| Pre-class readings & demos | this site (sidebar, by unit) |
| Reading quizzes | LMS, due before each class |
| Homework notebooks | course repo `homework/`, opened in Colab or Jupyter |
| The toolbox | `%pip install git+https://github.com/YOURUSERNAME/fluidtools` |
| Tool documentation | [Tools](tools.qmd) page |

No textbook is required — these pages are the course text. If you want to
hear another voice covering the same topics, *Munson's Fundamentals of
Fluid Mechanics* is at an appropriate level.
